newsitem.title: UK: Conservatives out but Thatcher's spirit lives on.
newsitem.headline: Conservatives out but Thatcher's spirit lives on.

text.p: She has been out of office for more than six years. Now her Conservative Party is in the political wilderness after 18 years ruling Britain.
But friends and foes alike agree on two things as Labour's Tony Blair prepares to take Britain into the new millennium.
Firstly, Margaret Thatcher presided over a revolution in British society and politics bigger than anything that had been seen since the welfare state was set up in the late 1940s.

Secondly her ideas triumphed so decisively that the revolution which continued under her successor, John Major, will be barely blunted by Tony Blair becoming prime minister after Labour's landslide win in Thursday's election.
"The terms of the debate have changed," said Madsen Pirie, president of the Adam Smith Institute, a right-wing free enterprise think-tank.
"The battle is won and now it is just a mopping-up operation. I fully expect that under Labour none of this will change. They have hauled down the red flag and pulled up the white one."
From the opposite end of the political spectrum, Richard Crockett, history and politics lecturer at London's Royal Holloway College, agrees.
"Thatcherism has become the hegemonic ideology of the era," he said. "Now we judge our elections on which party can better prepare Britain for life in the harsh jungle of the global free market."
When Thatcher came to power in 1979, many key British key industries -- telecommunications, steel, electricity, gas, water, even some car factories -- were in public ownership.
Inflation was in double figures, and repeated efforts by both Labour and Conservative governments to tame it through incomes policies had broken down.

The trade unions had just destroyed the latest attempt with a "winter of discontent" in which rubbish had rotted in the streets and the dead had lain unburied because of vicious public sector strikes.
All that has changed through massive privatisations, the ending of foreign exchange controls, a crackdown on public spending and huge changes to labour laws.
"You could not go through a day in 1979 without encountering the government in all its myriad forms," he said. "These days you can go for weeks on end without encountering the state at all."
But other analysts point to the cost of these changes.
In 1979, they argue, most Britons had adequately-paid jobs which they believed would be theirs until retirement, with full employment contracts giving them holiday, sickness and pension rights.
They could look forward to support from an all-embracing welfare state if misfortune struck at them or their families.

Welfare rights have since been shaved in the drive to cut government spending and nowadays many jobs are on short fixed-term contracts enabling employers to evade previously traditional obligations to their workers.
For most of the Conservative period, unemployment has been close to or above two million, against 1.3 million in 1979.
The Thatcher revolution, coinciding as it has with the collapse of Communism as a world force, has touched everything -- even the Conservatives' political opponents.
While Labour's immediate response to loss of office in 1979 was to adopt a left-wing socialist line, it has gradually accommodated itself to the new orthodoxy.
Blair completed this process in 1994 with the highly symbolic ditching of Clause Four of the Labour Party constitution, with its commitment to "common ownership of the means of production".
"It is the most sincere form of flattery that Labour are taking over most Conservative tenets," said Bill Rubinstein, the U.S.-born professor of history at the University of Wales.
Gloomy left-wing academics and journalists see Labour's transformation as the ultimate victory of Thatcherism, which guarantee its continued triumph despite the voters' verdict.

"None of the big reforms of the Thatcher years -- trade union reform, privatisation and the huge reductions in taxation for the better-off -- will be challenged," columnist Larry Elliott wrote in the Guardian.
"Labour shares the (outgoing Conservative) government's obsession with free markets, free trade and competition."
